title: Adding your own data tracks
blurb: This tutorial introduces you to the Track Manager view, where you can register your own tracks and attach them to a genome. It demonstrates this for a few different data types and shows how to subsequently view them in the Genome Browser.
completionBody: You can now bring your own data into Ensembl Go and read it beside the genes. Your own registered tracks were never touched, and the tutorial's temporary data has been cleared away.

steps.title: Bringing your own data
steps.body: Ensembl Go can draw your own data files beside a genome's annotation — coverage, peaks, variants. This tutorial registers three of them from a small demo set, then reads each one in the browser. Next advances each step if you would rather read than do.

steps.title: Open the Track Manager
steps.body: Everything you add starts here. Press Track Manager — or press Next and the tutorial will press it for you.

steps.title: What it is for
steps.body: A track is a data file the browser draws under the genes. Registering one records where it lives, what kind of data it holds and which genome it belongs to — it does not copy or move the file.

steps.title: Add Track
steps.body: This is the one control that starts a registration. It opens a short wizard: choose a file, say what it is, and it joins the list below.

steps.title: The Track Hub Registry
steps.body: Below your own tracks, the app looks your active genomes up in the Track Hub Registry. Where a hub publishes data for one of them, it can be imported from here without your having to find and download the files.

steps.title: Start a registration
steps.body: We have put three demo data files in the tutorial's own folder. Press Add Track to register the first of them — or press Next.

steps.title: The registration wizard
steps.body: Two steps: find the file, then describe it. Nothing is written until you press Register at the end, so you can change your mind about any of it.

steps.title: Find the file
steps.body: Press Browse for file to open the app's file browser — or press Next and the tutorial will open it for you.

steps.title: The demo data folder
steps.body: The browser has opened in the tutorial's own folder, which holds the three demo files. It lists only the types a track can be made from, so anything you can see here is something the app can draw.

steps.title: Pick the expression file
steps.body: ‘brain_expression.bw’ is RNA-seq coverage from brain tissue. Choose it — or press Next and the tutorial will choose it for you.

steps.title: What it found
steps.body: The file is in, and the type was read off its extension — BigWig, a compressed signal format. The label has been filled in from the filename, and everything below it describes how the track will be drawn.

steps.title: Name it
steps.body: The label is what you will see in the browser's left-hand panel and in the list of tracks to add, so it is worth making it readable. Type ‘Brain expression’ — or press Next.

steps.title: What kind of data
steps.body: A BigWig is just numbers along a chromosome, so the app cannot tell coverage from accessibility. Telling it this is RNA-seq is what picks a sensible way to draw it. Choose RNA-seq — or press Next.

steps.title: Zoned heatmap
steps.body: RNA-seq brings Zoned Heatmap with it. Expression spans orders of magnitude, so the track is banded rather than plotted: four bands at 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000, each with its own colour.

steps.title: Which genome
steps.body: This is the field to get right, and we have filled it in with the demo slice. A track left with no genome is registered and then never drawn — the browser only offers tracks belonging to the genome in front of you.

steps.title: Register it
steps.body: Press Register Track. The file is checked and, for formats that need one, an index is built beside it — so this can take a moment. Or press Next.

steps.title: It is in the list
steps.body: The wizard has closed and the track is on the page, under a heading for the genome it belongs to. The badge is its file type, and the line beneath tells you how it will be drawn.

steps.title: The ATAC-seq track
steps.body: The second file, ‘atac_seq_peaks.bw’, is also a BigWig — open chromatin from adrenal gland. Same two steps: find it, describe it. Press Next to fill the file step in.

steps.title: A different kind of signal
steps.body: The same file type, and a different answer here changes the picture completely: ATAC-seq brings Signal Plot instead, because peaks are read by their shape rather than their order of magnitude. Choose ATAC-seq — or press Next.

steps.title: Set, and different
steps.body: Signal Plot, and a colour of its own. The same two files would be drawn the same way if we had answered the same way twice — the picture follows the answer, not the format. Label and genome are filled in, so this one is ready.

steps.title: Register it too
steps.body: Genome chosen, label set. Press Register Track — or press Next.

steps.title: The variant track
steps.body: The last file is ‘variants.vcf.gz’ — 81,830 variants across this region, from Ensembl. Choose it — or press Next.

steps.title: A VCF needs an index
steps.body: A VCF is read in pieces rather than all at once, so it needs a tabix index beside it. Ours came with one; where it has not, the app builds it when you register. The two colours separate variants inside a gene from those between genes.

steps.title: Three registered
steps.body: All three are on the page now, grouped under the genome they belong to. Registering them is as far as the Track Manager goes — none of them is on screen in the browser yet.

steps.title: Open the Genome Browser
steps.body: Press Genome Browser — or press Next. The demo slice is already active, so it opens on a region of human chromosome 1.

steps.title: Registering is not showing
steps.body: This button in the genome's own toolbar is how a registered track gets onto the panel. Keeping the two apart means a track you rarely want is registered once and added only when you need it.

steps.title: Open the picker
steps.body: Press it — or press Next and the tutorial will press it for you.

steps.title: What is available
steps.body: Only tracks registered against this genome are offered, which is the genome field from the wizard doing its work. Each row shows the type, the label you gave it and where the file is.

steps.title: Tick all three
steps.body: Tick each of the three — or press Next and the tutorial will tick whichever you have not. Nothing is added until the button below, so this is only a choice.

steps.title: Add them
steps.body: Press Add — or press Next. The count on the button is how many are ticked.

steps.title: Three new tracks
steps.body: They are drawn under the genes, in the order they were added, and each is marked CT in the left-hand panel. We are looking at PHGDH and HMGCS2, about 115 kb of chromosome 1.

steps.title: Orders of magnitude
steps.body: The expression track is banded, not plotted. Each band is a decade — 100, 1,000, 10,000, 100,000 — so how many are filled tells you the order of magnitude, and the colour says it again from yellow through orange to red.

steps.title: Down to the exons
steps.body: Press Next to travel in to two of PHGDH's exons. You can also drag the track sideways or use the arrow keys, and zoom with the wheel or + and −.

steps.title: Where the reads are
steps.body: The signal sits on the exons and drops between them — this is RNA, so it follows what was transcribed rather than the DNA underneath. Over the exon on the right it reaches 1,440, filling three of the four bands.

steps.title: A plot of peaks
steps.body: The ATAC-seq track is drawn as an ordinary signal plot, one height per position. ATAC-seq marks chromatin loose enough for proteins to reach, so its peaks tend to fall where genes are switched on rather than along their length.

steps.title: A shared promoter
steps.body: Press Next to travel to the tallest peak in this region. It is worth a look for where it lands rather than for its height.

steps.title: Between two genes
steps.body: ZNF697 ends here and PHGDH begins, pointing opposite ways, and the peak sits in the gap between them — one stretch of open chromatin serving both. Reading two tracks together is the point of having them side by side.

steps.title: Blocks, not variants
steps.body: At this width there are far too many variants to draw one by one, so the track counts them into blocks — each one 500 bases here — and shades the block by how many it holds.

steps.title: The blocks get finer
steps.body: Press Next to zoom in. The track redraws at a finer grain as you go — five levels of detail in all, chosen from how much of the chromosome is on screen.

steps.title: A hundred bases a block
steps.body: Twenty kilobases on screen, and the blocks are a hundred bases each. Still counts rather than variants — but the shape of where variation clusters is already readable.

steps.title: All the way in
steps.body: Press Next to go to the bases. Below about five kilobases the track stops counting and draws every variant as its own mark.

steps.title: One mark each
steps.body: Three hundred bases, and 129 variants in them — mostly single-base changes, with five deletions and an insertion among them. The sequence is drawn underneath, and PHGDH's exon runs through the middle.

steps.title: Try one
steps.body: Hover a mark to pick it out, and click it for its identifier, its type and its alleles. A deletion is worth clicking: it keeps one anchor base and highlights every base it removes, so you can see its extent on the sequence below.

steps.title: The left-hand panel
steps.body: Every track has a switch here, the custom ones marked CT. A track can also be dragged up or down from here, to sit next to whatever you are comparing it with.

steps.title: Switch two off
steps.body: Turn the ATAC-seq and variant tracks off with their switches, leaving the expression one on — or press Next and the tutorial will do it.

steps.title: Off, but still there
steps.body: Both rows have gone blank and kept their place — the switch stops a track being drawn, it does not take it off the panel. The expression track carries on, and nothing has been unregistered.

steps.title: Hide
steps.body: Hide, in the bar that applies to every genome, takes the empty rows away as well. Press it — or press Next.

steps.title: The space comes back
steps.body: The two switched-off rows are gone entirely and the panel has closed up around what is left. Useful once a genome has more tracks than you are reading at once.

steps.title: And back
steps.body: The same button reads Show while it is on. Press it to bring the empty rows back — or press Next.

steps.title: Nothing was lost
steps.body: All three rows are back, with the two still switched off. Hiding and switching off are both about what you are looking at; neither touches what is registered.

steps.title: Where the demo data stops
steps.body: These three files cover 220 kb around PHGDH, rather than the whole slice, so that they are small enough to ship with the app. Pan far enough either way and the tracks run out while the genes carry on — your own files will have their own edges.

steps.title: What you have done
steps.body: We registered three files in the Track Manager — naming each one, saying what kind of data it held and which genome it belonged to — then added them to a browser panel and read all three: banded expression over PHGDH's exons, an ATAC-seq peak in a shared promoter, and a variant track from counted blocks down to single bases. Then we switched two off from the left-hand panel and used Hide to close the space up.
